claim: The medial subnucleus of the amygdala (MeA) plays a central role in processing sensory cues required for innate behaviors.
source: The medial subnucleus of the amygdala (MeA) plays a central role in processing sensory cues required for innate behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational claim about MeA function, supported by the broader literature context.

claim: The telencephalic preoptic area (POA) embryonic niche is a novel source of MeA destined progenitors.
source: Our previous studies revealed that the telencephalic preoptic area (POA) embryonic niche is a novel source of MeA destined progenitors.
evidence: This claim references previous studies by the authors establishing the POA as a source of MeA progenitors.

claim: The POA is comprised of distinct progenitor pools complementarily marked by the transcription factors Dbx1 and Foxp2.
source: Here, we show that the POA is comprised of distinct progenitor pools complementarily marked by the transcription factors Dbx1 and Foxp2.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Embryonic parcellation by Dbx1 and Foxp2 predicts postnatal MeA inhibitory neuronal subtype identity based on molecular and electrophysiological criteria.
source: As determined by molecular and electrophysiological criteria this embryonic parcellation predicts postnatal MeA inhibitory neuronal subtype identity.
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular marker analysis (Figure 2, 4) and electrophysiological recordings (Figure 3) presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ cells in the MeA are differentially activated in response to innate behavioral cues in a sex-specific manner.
source: We further find that Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ cells in the MeA are differentially activated in response to innate behavioral cues in a sex-specific manner.
evidence: This is supported by c-fos activation studies during behavioral assays shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: The MeA serves as a hub in integrating conspecific and non-conspecific environmental cues with social and survival salience to generate appropriate behavioral responses.
source: The medial subnucleus of the amygdala (MeA) serves as a hub in this function, residing only two synapses away from sensory neurons in the vomeronasal organ (Dulac and Wagner, 2006; Sokolowski and Corbin, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature establishing MeA function.

claim: The MeA resides only two synapses away from sensory neurons in the vomeronasal organ.
source: The medial subnucleus of the amygdala (MeA) serves as a hub in this function, residing only two synapses away from sensory neurons in the vomeronasal organ (Dulac and Wagner, 2006; Sokolowski and Corbin, 2012).
evidence: This anatomical claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The MeA along with the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST) and multiple nuclei of the hypothalamus form a core limbic circuit largely dedicated to processing innate behaviors.
source: The MeA along with the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST) and multiple nuclei of the hypothalamus including the ventromedial hypothalamus, form a core limbic circuit largely dedicated to processing innate behaviors (Dulac and Wagner, 2006; Gross and Canteras, 2012; Choi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim about circuit organization is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Classical studies revealed a central role for the MeA in the regulation of innate behaviors such as aggression, mating and predator avoidance.
source: Classical studies investigating patterns of neuronal activation in response to behavioral or olfactory cues (Kollack and Newman, 1992; Erskine, 1993), lesioning studies (Vochteloo and Koolhaas, 1987; Takahashi and Gladstone, 1988; Kondo, 1992) and more recent optogenetic approaches (Hong et al., 2014) have revealed a central role for the MeA in the regulation of innate behaviors such as aggression, mating and predator avoidance.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to classical and recent studies.

claim: The MeA is one of many known sexually dimorphic regions of the brain, with differences in numbers of neurons, glia, and synaptic organization between males and females.
source: In addition to the processing of innate cues, the MeA is one of many known sexually dimorphic regions of the brain, with differences in numbers of neurons, glia, and synaptic organization between males and females (Cooke and Woolley, 2005; Johnson et al., 2008; McCarthy and Arnold, 2011).
evidence: This claim about sexual dimorphism is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The MeA expresses high levels of steroid hormone pathway proteins such as aromatase, estrogen receptor and androgen receptor.
source: The critical role that the MeA plays in regulating sex-specific behaviors is reflected in the high expression levels of steroid hormone pathway proteins such as aromatase, estrogen receptor and androgen receptor (Wu et al., 2009; Juntti et al., 2010; Unger et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing hormone receptor expression.

claim: MeA neuronal subpopulations expressing different combinations of steroid hormone pathway proteins regulate aggression or mating behaviors in male and female mice.
source: MeA neuronal subpopulations expressing different combinations of these proteins have been shown to regulate aggression or mating behaviors in male and female mice (Juntti et al., 2010; Hong et al., 2014; Unger et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: Progenitors located at the telencephalic-diencephalic border are a major source of MeA neuronal populations.
source: Previous studies of MeA development revealed that progenitors located at the telencephalic-diencephalic border are a major source of MeA neuronal populations (Zhao et al., 2008; Hirata et al., 2009; Soma et al., 2009; García-Moreno et al., 2010).
evidence: This developmental claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Dbx1 expression defines a progenitor population that generates a subclass of MeA putative inhibitory projection neurons.
source: Our previous work revealed that one of these progenitor populations is defined by the transient expression of the developmentally regulated transcription factor, Dbx1, which in turn generates a subclass of MeA putative inhibitory projection neurons (Hirata et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim references the authors' previous work establishing Dbx1+ progenitor contribution to MeA.

claim: The MeA is comprised of diverse populations of local interneurons and both excitatory and inhibitory output neurons.
source: However, the MeA is also comprised of diverse populations of local interneurons and both excitatory and inhibitory output neurons (Bian, 2013; Keshavarzi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim about MeA neuronal diversity is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Foxp2 is a forkhead transcription factor implicated in the development and function of neurons and required in motor coordinating centers for appropriate production of speech.
source: Here, we demonstrate that in addition to Dbx1 expression, a subset of MeA embryonic progenitors are complementarily marked by expression of Foxp2, a forkhead transcription factor implicated in the development and function of neurons and required in the motor coordinating centers of the brain for the appropriate production of speech (French and Fisher, 2014).
evidence: This claim about Foxp2 function is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Embryonic Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ progenitor populations are non-overlapping during embryogenesis.
source: Interestingly, during embryogenesis, Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ progenitor populations were non-overlapping (Figure 1a–l).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1a-l and quantified in the Venn diagrams.

claim: Both Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ populations are generally distinct from OTP+ progenitors.
source: Both populations were also generally distinct from OTP+ progenitors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–i), a population previously shown to define a subset of MeA-fated progenitors (García-Moreno et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work on OTP.

claim: Embryonic Foxp2+ cells are not derived from Shh or Nkx6.2 lineages (~5% overlap).
source: We found embryonic Foxp2+ cells were not derived from either lineage (~5% overlap) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) further expanding our knowledge of the molecular diversity of the MeA niche.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic fate-mapping data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The segregation of Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ cells persists into adulthood across the rostro-caudal extent of the postnatal MeA.
source: Interestingly, this embryonic molecular parcellation persisted into adulthood as Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ cells remained non-overlapping across the rostro-caudal extent of the postnatal MeA (Figure 1m–r; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in adult brains shown in Figure 1m-r and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Postnatally, Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ neurons remain distinct from OTP+ cells.
source: Similarly, postnatally, the Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ neurons remained distinct from OTP+ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1j–x).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in postnatal brains shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1j-x.

claim: 81% ± 2.6 of Foxp2+ cells express NeuN, a pan neuronal marker.
source: Our analysis revealed that 81% ± 2.6 of Foxp2+ cells expressed NeuN, a pan neuronal marker (Mullen et al., 1992) (Figure 2a–d)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2a-d.

claim: None of the Foxp2+ cells co-express the oligodendrocyte marker CC1.
source: with none co-expressing the oligodendrocyte marker, CC1 (Koenning et al., 2012) (Figure 2e–h).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2e-h.

claim: Only 3% ± 1.2 of Foxp2+ cells are derived from the Emx1-lineage, a broad marker of excitatory neurons.
source: We found that only 3% ± 1.2 of Foxp2+ cells were derived from the Emx1-lineage, a broad marker of excitatory neurons (Gorski et al., 2002) (Figure 2i–l).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic fate-mapping data shown in Figure 2i-l.

claim: 22% ± 6.6 of Foxp2+ cells express the inhibitory marker Calbindin.
source: We further found that 22% ± 6.6 of Foxp2+ cells expressed the inhibitory marker Calbindin (Figure 2m–p)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2m-p.

claim: 15% ± 2.5 of Foxp2+ cells express nNOS.
source: with a smaller percentage of Foxp2+ cells (15% ± 2.5) expressing nNOS (Figure 2q–t)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2q-t.

claim: 5% ± 0.6 of Foxp2+ cells express somatostatin.
source: or somatostatin (5% ± 0.6) (Figure 2u–x)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2u-x.

claim: Foxp2+ MeA cells are not excitatory and are likely inhibitory.
source: Collectively, although we did not fully assess all putative inhibitory markers, these data reveal that Foxp2+ MeA are not excitatory and are likely inhibitory (Figure 2y).
evidence: This is an inference based on the molecular marker data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The majority (19/28) of Dbx1-derived neurons are characterized by a regular, tonic spiking pattern with 3–4 spikes at rheobase.
source: Here, we found that the majority (19/28) of Dbx1-derived neurons were characterized by a regular, tonic spiking pattern with 3–4 spikes at rheobase (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The majority (15/23) of Foxp2+ neurons are distinguished by a phasic firing pattern and display a single or double spike upon repolarization after hyperpolarization.
source: In contrast, the majority (15/23) of Foxp2+ neurons were distinguished by a phasic firing pattern and displayed a single or double spike upon repolarization after hyperpolarization, a profile characteristic of inhibitory neurons (Llinás, 1988) (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3b and citation to previous literature.

claim: Dbx1-derived and Foxp2-derived neurons display significant differences in resting membrane potential, input resistance, capacitance, and action potential frequency but not in rheobase.
source: Dbx1-derived and Foxp2-derived neurons (confirmed Foxp2+ by immunohistochemistry) also displayed significant differences in resting membrane potential, input resistance, capacitance, and action potential frequency but not in rheobase (Figure 3c–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3c-g.

claim: Foxp2+ neurons possess dendritic spines, suggesting they are projection neurons similar to Dbx1-derived neurons.
source: In addition, the presence of spines in Foxp2+ neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) suggested that similar to Dbx1-derived neurons, Foxp2+ neurons are projection neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on morphological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dbx1-derived neurons receive significantly more frequent and greater amplitude sEPSCs than Foxp2+ neurons.
source: Dbx1-derived neurons received significantly more frequent and greater amplitude of sEPSCs than Foxp2+ neurons (Figure 3h–l).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings of sEPSCs shown in Figure 3h-l.

claim: Dbx1-derived MeA neurons receive a greater number and/or stronger excitatory inputs than Foxp2+ neurons.
source: This suggests that Dbx1-derived MeA neurons receive a greater number and/or stronger excitatory inputs than Foxp2+ neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sEPSC data.

claim: Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ cells in males express ERα to the same extent (28.4% ± 4.8 in Dbx1-derived cells; 24.0% ± 7.2 in Foxp2+ cells).
source: We found that Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ cells in males expressed ERα to the same extent (28.4% ± 4.8 in Dbx1-derived cells; 24.0% ± 7.2 in Foxp2+ cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4a-g.

claim: Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ cells in females show significant differences in ERα expression (45% ± 3.4 in Dbx1-derived cells; 24.8% ± 5.8 in Foxp2+ cells).
source: However, Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ cells in females showed significant differences in ERα expression (45% ± 3.4 in Dbx1-derived cells; 24.8% ± 5.8 in Foxp2+ cells) (Figure 4a–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4a-g.

claim: The majority of Dbx1-derived cells express aromatase both in males (61.7% ± 7.6) and females (52.4% ± 5.2).
source: The majority of Dbx1-derived cells expressed aromatase both in males (61.7% ± 7.6) and females (52.4% ± 5.2), which was at a significantly higher percentage than in Foxp2+ cells in males (0.12% ± 0) and females (7.2% ± 6.0) (Figure 4h–n).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4h-n.

claim: Foxp2+ cells express aromatase at significantly lower percentages than Dbx1-derived cells in males (0.12% ± 0) and females (7.2% ± 6.0).
source: The majority of Dbx1-derived cells expressed aromatase both in males (61.7% ± 7.6) and females (52.4% ± 5.2), which was at a significantly higher percentage than in Foxp2+ cells in males (0.12% ± 0) and females (7.2% ± 6.0) (Figure 4h–n).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4h-n.

claim: There are no subpopulation differences in AR expression between Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ neurons in both males and females.
source: There were no subpopulation differences in AR expression as both Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ neurons in both males (26.8% ± 4.1 in Dbx1-derived cells; 16.2% ± 3.2 in Foxp2+ cells) and females (8.4% ± 3.6 in Dbx1-derived cells; 7.0% ± 1.8 in Foxp2+ cells) co-expressed AR at the same levels (Figure 4o–u).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4o-u.

claim: A greater percentage of Dbx1-derived cells in males (26.8% ± 4.1) express AR than Dbx1-derived cells in females (8.4% ± 3.6).
source: However, there were sex-specific differences observed as a greater percentage of Dbx1-derived cells in males (26.8% ± 4.1) expressed AR than Dbx1-derived cells in females (8.4% ± 3.6).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4o-u.

claim: There is a significant increase in the number of c-fos+ cells in the MeA during male territorial aggression compared to naïve mice.
source: Concordant with previous literature (Wang et al., 2013), we found a significant increase in the number of c-fos+ cells in the MeA in comparison to naïve mice (Figure 5a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5a-c and citation to previous literature.

claim: Both the number and proportion of activated Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ subpopulations in males are significantly increased during territorial aggression compared to control mice.
source: In addition, both the number and proportion of activated Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ subpopulations in males were significantly increased during territorial aggression compared to control (naïve) mice (Figure 5d–k,x).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5d-k,x.

claim: There is a significant increase in the number of c-fos+ cells in the MeA during maternal aggression compared to both stressed and naïve controls.
source: We found a significant increase in the number of c-fos+ cells in the MeA in the maternal aggression condition compared to both stressed and naïve controls (Figure 5l–o).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5l-o.

claim: Both the number and proportion of activated Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ subpopulations significantly increase during maternal aggression in comparison to the naïve condition.
source: When examining subtype-specific levels of activation, we found that both the number and proportion of activated Dbx1-derived and the Foxp2+ subpopulations significantly increased during maternal aggression in comparison to the naïve condition (Figure 5p–w,y).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5p-w,y.

claim: There is an increase in c-fos+ cells in the MeA during both male and female mating.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Rowe and Erskine, 1993), we observed an increase in c-fos+ cells in the MeA during both male and female mating (Figure 6a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6a-c and citation to previous literature.

claim: The number and proportion of the activated Dbx1-derived subpopulation is significantly increased during both male and female mating when compared to naïve controls.
source: While the number and proportion of the activated Dbx1-derived subpopulation was significantly increased during both male and female mating when compared to naïve controls (Figure 6d–g,l)
evidence: This claim is supported by c-fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6d-g,l.

claim: The number and proportion of activated Foxp2+ cells increase only during male but not during female mating.
source: the number and proportion of activated Foxp2+ cells increased only during male but not during female mating (Figure 6h–k,m).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6h-k,m.

claim: There is a significant increase in the number of c-fos+ cells in the MeA in response to predator odor in both male and female mice.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Canteras et al., 2015), in response to predator odor we observed a significant increase in the number of c-fos+ cells in the MeA in both male and female mice (Figure 7a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7a-c and citation to previous literature.

claim: Dbx1-derived cells in male and female mice are not activated in response to predator odor exposure in comparison to benign bedding.
source: Interestingly, the Dbx1-derived cells in male and female mice were not activated in response to predator odor exposure in comparison to the benign bedding (Figure 7d–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7d-g.

claim: A significant activation of Foxp2+ cells in comparison to controls is observed in female mice, but not in males, in response to predator odor.
source: In contrast, we observed a significant activation of Foxp2+ cells in comparison to controls in female mice, but not in males (Figure 7h–k).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7h-k.

claim: A greater number of OTP+ cells in both males and females are activated in response to predator odor.
source: We observed that a greater number of OTP+ cells in both males and females were activated in response to predator odor (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a significant increase in the OTP+ population in females in response to predator odor when analyzing the proportion of OTP+ cells activated.
source: When analyzing the proportion of OTP+ cells activated, we found no differences between the benign and the predator avoidance groups in males, but we did find a significant increase in the OTP+ population in females.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of c-fos data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The OTP+ population in the female brain is activated at a level above control in response to a strong aversive innate olfactory cue, in contrast to Dbx1-derived or Foxp2+ cells.
source: Therefore, in the female brain, the OTP+ population, in contrast to Dbx1-derived or Foxp2+ cells, were activated at a level above control in response to a strong aversive innate olfactory cue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the c-fos activation data comparing different cell populations.

claim: Differential transcription factor expression within the embryonic MeA progenitor niche predicts mature output neuronal subtype identity.
source: Integrating genetic fate-mapping, patch clamp electrophysiology and animal behavioral assays we uncover a fundamental link between embryonic patterning and brain responses to innate behavioral cues at two levels: (1) differential transcription factor expression within the embryonic MeA progenitor niche predicts mature output neuronal subtype identity
evidence: This is a summary claim integrating multiple lines of evidence from the study.

claim: Embryonic transcription factor expression predicts subpopulation sex-specific responses to mating and predator odor avoidance cues.
source: and (2) further predicts subpopulation sex-specific responses to mating and predator odor avoidance cues.
evidence: This is a summary claim integrating behavioral activation data from the study.

claim: Transcription factor expression at the progenitor stage may be instructive for the establishment of neuronal populations and sub-circuits regulating sex-specific behaviors.
source: Our findings further suggest that transcription factor expression at the progenitor stage may be instructive for the establishment of neuronal populations and sub-circuits regulating sex-specific behaviors.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the findings of the study.

claim: The generation of neuronal diversity across amygdala subnuclei has been posited to occur in a compartmentalized manner with amygdala inhibitory neurons generated in the subpallial ganglionic eminences and excitatory neurons arising from the cortical pallial region.
source: The generation of neuronal diversity across amygdala subnuclei has been posited to occur in a compartmentalized manner with amygdala inhibitory neurons generated in the subpallial ganglionic eminences and excitatory neurons arising from the cortical pallial region (Swanson and Petrovich, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Recent studies have revealed that the generation of amygdala neuronal diversity is more complex with large populations of neurons originating in progenitor niches dedicated for limbic structures.
source: However, more recent studies have revealed that the generation of amygdala neuronal diversity is more complex with large populations of neurons originating in progenitor niches dedicated for limbic structures (Remedios et al., 2007; Hirata et al., 2009; Soma et al., 2009; Waclaw et al., 2010; García-Moreno et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple recent studies.

claim: One major niche for MeA neurons encompasses the region at the telencephalic-diencephalic border, an origin of MeA output neurons.
source: One of these major niches encompasses the region at the telencephalic-diencephalic border, an origin of MeA output neurons (Hirata et al., 2009; García-Moreno et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The function of combinatorial sets of transcription factors in neural progenitors has been shown across the neuraxis as the mechanism for the generation and specification of distinct subclasses of neurons.
source: The function of combinatorial sets of transcription factors in neural progenitors has been shown across the neuraxis as the mechanism for the generation and specification of distinct subclasses of neurons (Kepecs and Fishell, 2014; Stepien et al., 2010; Shirasaki and Pfaff, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Recent studies in the spinal cord and globus pallidus have revealed that different combinatorial codes in progenitor pools predict neuronal subtype connectivity patterns, neuronal firing properties and distinct functions.
source: In addition to specification of neuronal subtype identity, recent studies in the spinal cord and globus pallidus (Dodson et al., 2015; Bikoff et al., 2016) have revealed that different combinatorial codes in progenitor pools predict neuronal subtype connectivity patterns, neuronal firing properties and in the case of the globus pallidus, distinct functions in regulating voluntary movements (Dodson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Recent optogenetic manipulation of the MeA revealed that glutamatergic neurons mediate repetitive self-grooming behaviors while GABA-ergic neurons regulate either aggressive or mating behaviors, depending on the level of neuronal activity.
source: Recent optogenetic manipulation of the MeA revealed that glutamatergic neurons mediate repetitive self-grooming behaviors while in contrast GABA-ergic neurons regulate either aggressive or mating behaviors, depending on the level of neuronal activity driven by light stimulation (Hong et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous optogenetic study.

claim: MeA neuronal subclasses expressing different components of the stress response system control appropriate behavioral responses to social cues.
source: Moreover, MeA neuronal subclasses expressing different components of the stress response system control appropriate behavioral responses to social cues (Shemesh et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Recent studies employing in vivo recording techniques revealed that a significant number of MeA neurons are dedicated to processing olfactory cues from the opposite sex rather than the same-sex.
source: Recent studies employing in vivo recording techniques revealed that a significant number of MeA neurons are dedicated to processing olfactory cues from the opposite sex rather than the same-sex, thus providing a direct demonstration of sex-specific differences in sensory processing (Bergan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous in vivo recording study.

claim: In the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH), progesterone receptor-expressing neurons are required for male aggressive and mating behaviors, but only for female mating behavior.
source: A similar sex-specific control of innate behavior has been directly demonstrated in the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH), where progesterone receptor-expressing neurons while required for male aggressive and mating behaviors, are only required for female mating behavior (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on VMH.

claim: Sex steroid hormones and receptors such as aromatase, ERα and AR are critical for the output of distinct components of male and female aggressive and mating behaviors.
source: Regarding the first potential mechanism, sex steroid hormones and receptors such as aromatase, ERα and AR have been extensively characterized as critical for the output of distinct components of male and female aggressive and mating behaviors (Yang and Shah, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Deletion of AR resulted in alterations in attack duration during territorial aggression and initiation of male mating.
source: For example, deletion of AR resulted in alterations in attack duration during territorial aggression and initiation of male mating (Juntti et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous genetic study.

claim: Ablation of aromatase neurons led to impairments in the production of distinct components of aggression in male and female mice.
source: while ablation of aromatase neurons led to impairments in the production of distinct components of aggression in male and female mice (Unger et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous ablation study.

claim: Across species, aromatase has a masculinizing effect.
source: Across species, aromatase has a masculinizing effect (Wu et al., 2009; Balthazart et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The timing of AP spiking is directly linked to specific behavioral actions in both vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: Previous work in both vertebrates and invertebrates has revealed that the timing of AP spiking is directly linked to specific behavioral actions.
evidence: This is a general claim about neural coding supported by established knowledge.

claim: In vertebrates, timescale firing differences are associated with dopamine (DA) release for the determination of reward behaviors.
source: For example, in vertebrates timescale firing differences are associated with dopamine (DA) release for the determination of reward behaviors (Schultz, 2007; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on dopamine and reward.

claim: Sex-specific differences in connectivity have been observed in c. elegans where shared male and female circuits show differences in connectivity established during wiring.
source: Although currently not yet observed in a brain circuit in mammals, such a mechanism has recently been uncovered in c. elegans in which shared male and female circuits show differences in connectivity that is established during wiring (Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study in c. elegans.

claim: There is some suggestion of sex-specific differences in olfactory-MeA projections in rodents.
source: Consistent with this, there is some suggestion of sex-specific differences in olfactory-MeA projections in rodents (Kang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: There are direct excitatory inputs to the MeA emanating from the mitral/tufted neurons of the accessory olfactory bulb (AOB).
source: Although the source of input cannot be determined from our analysis, there are direct excitatory inputs to the MeA emanating from the mitral/tufted neurons of the accessory olfactory bulb (AOB) (Martel and Baum, 2009; Bergan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Foxp2+ precursors in the VZ are observed putatively migrating to the SVZ at E11.5.
source: As shown at E11.5 (s) Foxp2+ precursors in the VZ (arrows) are observed putatively migrating to the SVZ.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 1s showing Foxp2+ cell distribution.

claim: 1% ± 0.4 of OTP+ cells are derived from the Emx1-lineage.
source: We found that 1% ± 0.4 of OTP+ cells were derived from the Emx1-lineage
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic fate-mapping data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: 13.5% ± 9.1 of OTP+ cells co-express CAMKIIα.
source: and 13.5% ± 9.1 co-expressed CAMKIIα (Jones et al., 1994), both excitatory markers.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: 56% ± 18.9 of OTP+ cells co-express calbindin.
source: In contrast, we observed 56% ± 18.9 of OTP+ cells co-expressed calbindin
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: 0% ± 0.1 of OTP+ cells co-express somatostatin.
source: while none (0% ± 0.1) co-expressed somatostatin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The majority of OTP+ cells appear to be inhibitory, similar to Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ neurons.
source: Therefore, similar to Dbx1-derived and Foxp2+ neurons, the majority of OTP+ cells appear to be inhibitory.
evidence: This is an inference based on the molecular marker data for OTP+ cells.
